report_name: Cisco Talos uncovers 'JWR' phishing framework with live operator steering

threat_actors.name: Chinese-speaking threat actors
threat_actors.description: Assessed with medium confidence by Cisco Talos to be the operators of the JWR and 'The Outsider' Phishing-as-a-Service (PhaaS) platforms, based on code similarities and language artifacts in the operator console.

attack_patterns.name: Spearphishing Link
attack_patterns.description: The JWR framework is used in smishing campaigns that deliver lures via SMS links to victims.

attack_patterns.name: Steal Web Session Cookie
attack_patterns.description: The JWR framework acts as a real-time proxy, allowing it to capture session cookies after a successful login to hijack the victim's session.

attack_patterns.name: Multi-Factor Authentication Interception
attack_patterns.description: The live, operator-driven nature of the JWR framework allows attackers to guide victims through MFA steps and steal 2FA codes in real-time, effectively bypassing this control.

attack_patterns.name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
attack_patterns.description: JWR is an Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) phishing framework that acts as a real-time proxy and interactive console for the attacker.

attack_patterns.name: Web Protocols
attack_patterns.description: The JWR framework uses an AES-CTR encrypted WebSocket connection for persistent, bidirectional communication between the victim and the attacker's server.

attack_patterns.name: Input Capture
attack_patterns.description: The live operator using the JWR framework can see everything the victim types into form fields in real-time, capturing credentials, 2FA codes, and other sensitive data.

malware.name: JWR
malware.description: A sophisticated phishing-as-a-service (PhaaS) framework that enables live, operator-driven Adversary-in-the-Middle (AiTM) attacks via an encrypted WebSocket channel to steal credentials, 2FA codes, and personal documents.

malware.name: The Outsider
malware.description: A Phishing-as-a-Service (PhaaS) platform that the JWR framework is assessed to be a variant of.

identities.name: Shopify
identities.description: A major brand impersonated by the JWR phishing framework to lure victims into fake login or checkout processes.

identities.name: PayPal
identities.description: A major brand impersonated by the JWR phishing framework to lure victims into fake login or checkout processes.

identities.description: A major brand impersonated by the JWR phishing framework to lure victims into fake login or checkout processes.

identities.description: A major brand impersonated by the JWR phishing framework to lure victims into fake login or checkout processes.

infrastructure.name: JWR Phishing Infrastructure
infrastructure.description: Attacker-controlled servers that host the phishing pages and manage the encrypted WebSocket connections for live operator interaction.

indicators.name: Suspicious Outbound WebSocket Connection
indicators.pattern:
title: Suspicious Outbound WebSocket Connection
id: d3a4b5c6-e7f8-4a9b-8c7d-6f5e4d3c2b1a
status: experimental
description: Detects outbound WebSocket (wss://) connections to new or uncategorized domains, which could indicate the use of an interactive phishing framework like JWR.
references:
  - https://blog.talosintelligence.com/dissecting-the-jwr-phishing-framework/
author: cyber.netsecops.io
date: 2026-08-14
tags:
  - attack.t1071.001
  - attack.command_and_control
level: medium
logsource:
  category: proxy
detection:
  selection:
    c-uri|startswith: 'wss://'
  filter_known_good:
    cs-host|endswith:
      - '.live.com'
      - '.microsoft.com'
      - '.office.com'
      - '.office365.com'
      - '.slack.com'
      - '.discord.com'
      - '.google.com'
      - '.zoom.us'
  condition: selection and not filter_known_good
indicators.description: Detects outbound WebSocket (wss://) connections to new or uncategorized domains, a behavior associated with the JWR phishing framework.
